newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg tops up dikes ahead of flood crest.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg tops up dikes ahead of flood crest.

text.p: Winnipeggers rushed to shore up dikes with a million more sandbags on Thursday as Red River waters were expected to crest later in the day.

"We were supposed to get more bags but this is all we've got. I hope it'll be enough," Harriette Shore said as 30 of her tenants laid 500 sandbags at her riverfront high-rise apartment building entrance. City surveyors forecast floodwaters would lap at the back door by Thursday's crest.
Shore's tenants were among 10,000 Winnipeggers put on 24-hour evacuation standby on Wednesday. The Red River flood, the worst in 145 years, has displaced 29,000 Canadians so far.

About 8,800 Winnipeggers have fled their homes as the rising river seeped through dikes shielding five city streets on Wednesday. Three homes flooded overnight and hundreds more remained empty, Winnipeg spokesman Nick Iafolla said.

The Manitoba capital, home to 650,000 people, is protected by a 29-mile (47-km) ditch parting the rising "Red Sea" and a 25-mile (40-km) dike southwest of the city that was completed on Wednesday. Authorities are worried the hastily built dike may break under the pressure of the river, which has flooded 800 square miles (2,100 sq km) of Manitoba land.

Engineers said Red River headwaters might reach Winnipeg within six hours of a breach of the dike, raising the river's crest two feet (60 cm) above its forecast peak downtown within 40 hours. Winnipeg's mayor on Wednesday ordered crews to add two more feet (60 cm) of sandbags to parts of the city's 75-mile (120-km) permanent earthen dike.

"We're adding two feet of sandbag protection to our primary dike streets," Winnipeg city engineer Jack Marquardson said. "I suppose we would be sacrificing the few homes on the riverside of the primary dike."

Other dikes were being shored up on Thursday morning behind the first line of defence. "The sandbags are on the boulevard purely as a secondary line of defence," Capt. Mark Leach said as soldiers put down 100,000 along a northeast Winnipeg riverside street.
So far 10 million sandbags were topping up dikes and temporary defences along 20 percent of the city's 150 miles (240 km) of riverbanks, Winnipeg Harbour Master Joe Pietracci said.

"Until the water starts to recede, we won't be able to get under the bridges. There could be 15 to 20 feet (4.5 to 6 metres) of headroom from the normal summer level to the bottom of the bridge," Pietracci said. "There's a cemetery that relocated 24 graves because it was possible they would break apart because of the high water."
River levels may remain high for two to four weeks, but the peak might recede from Winnipeg by Sunday, Manitoba Natural Resources flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said.
South winds were forecast to pose a threat to the dike southwest of Winnipeg on Sunday and an additional inch (2.5 cm) of rain could force an upward revision of the flood outlook, Whitney said.
South winds of up to 19 mph (30 kmh) were forecast for Manitoba on Sunday and about 0.2 inch (5 mm) of rain was expected on Monday, Environment Canada meteorologist Dale Marcisky said.
Normal precipitation for Winnipeg for the month of April is 1.4 inches (36 mm), but in May it is 2.4 inches (60 mm).
